stem: This week we are looking at how university courses are organized and what helps students succeed. Many universities record their lectures and post them online, so students can watch them at any time. Some instructors worry that this encourages students to skip class, while others think attendance should simply be a personal choice for adults. What do you think? Should universities require students to attend lectures in person, or should attendance be optional when recordings are available? Explain why.

posts.name: Priya
posts.text: I think attendance should be required. When I watch a recording at home, I am easily distracted by my phone and I often speed through the video without really thinking. In the lecture hall, I can ask the professor a question the moment I am confused, and that helps me understand difficult material much faster.

posts.name: Mateo
posts.text: In my view, attendance should be optional. Many students have part-time jobs or long commutes, and a strict attendance rule punishes them for reasons they cannot control. If a student can learn the material from a recording and still pass the exams, I don't see why the university should force them to sit in a room at a fixed time.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I understand Mateo's point about students with jobs, but I still believe universities should require attendance for most lectures. My main reason is that learning at a university is not only about receiving information; it is also about learning from classmates. In a live lecture, students hear the questions that other people ask, and these questions often reveal problems they had not noticed themselves. Recordings rarely capture this, because the microphone usually picks up only the professor. In addition, attending class builds a routine. When I have a fixed time for a course each week, I keep up with the readings, whereas recordings make it very easy to postpone everything until the night before the exam. That said, universities could allow a small number of absences each term for students with work or family duties. This would keep the benefits of attendance while remaining fair to people in difficult situations.
points: States a clear position in the first sentence and keeps it throughout
Adds a new reason (learning from classmates' questions, building a routine) instead of repeating Priya's point about asking questions
Responds directly to Mateo by name and offers a fair compromise
Uses linking words such as 'In addition', 'whereas' and 'That said' to connect ideas

stem: In our unit on workplace management, we have been discussing new ways of organizing working time. Several companies have tested a four-day work week, in which employees work four longer days or four normal days with no loss of pay. Supporters say it improves productivity and well-being, but critics argue that it does not suit every type of business. In your opinion, would a four-day work week be good for most companies and their employees? Why or why not?

posts.name: Kwame
posts.text: I think a four-day week would benefit most companies. When people know they have a long weekend coming, they focus harder and waste less time in unnecessary meetings. Rested employees also make fewer mistakes, so the company may actually produce more in four days than it used to produce in five.

posts.name: Sofia
posts.text: I disagree. A four-day week might work in an office, but many businesses, such as hospitals, shops and restaurants, need staff every day. If everyone works only four days, these companies must hire extra workers to cover the missing day, which raises their costs and could make prices higher for customers.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on business. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Sofia makes a good point about hospitals and shops, but I believe a four-day week would still be good for most companies, as long as it is introduced flexibly. One benefit that has not been mentioned is hiring. Today, many skilled workers can choose between several employers, and a shorter week is a very attractive benefit that costs less than a large salary increase. A company that offers it can attract talented people and keep them longer, which saves a great deal of money on recruiting and training new staff. Furthermore, businesses that need to stay open every day do not have to close for a day. They can schedule employees on different days, so the shop is always staffed while each person still works four days. Of course, every company should test the idea for a few months first and measure the results before making it permanent.
points: Takes a clear position and qualifies it ('as long as it is introduced flexibly')
Adds a new reason (attracting and keeping skilled workers) not given by Kwame or Sofia
Answers Sofia's objection by name with a practical solution (rotating schedules)
Ends with a sensible suggestion that rounds off the argument

stem: Our sociology course has been examining what makes a neighborhood feel like a real community. Researchers have found that people who know their neighbors tend to feel safer and more satisfied with where they live. However, in many modern cities, residents hardly speak to the people next door. Which do you think does more to build a sense of community in a neighborhood: shared physical spaces, such as parks and community gardens, or organized events, such as street festivals and clubs? Explain your choice.

posts.name: Amara
posts.text: Shared spaces matter most. A park or a community garden is there every single day, so neighbors meet again and again in a natural way. In my neighborhood, people started chatting at the new playground while their children played, and now they help each other with shopping and childcare. An event happens once, but a place keeps bringing people together.

posts.name: Lucas
posts.text: I believe organized events are more effective. Many people walk through a park without ever talking to anyone. An event gives them a reason to start a conversation, because everyone is there for the same activity. When my town held a cooking festival, I met more neighbors in one afternoon than I had in two years of living there.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Both Amara and Lucas raise good points, but I agree with Amara that shared spaces do more to build community. My reason is that spaces include people who would never sign up for an event. Shy residents, elderly people living alone, or newcomers who do not speak the local language well may feel uncomfortable at a festival full of strangers. A community garden, however, lets them join slowly. They can water their own plants, nod to the person at the next plot, and gradually start talking when they feel ready. Over time, these small, repeated contacts create trust, which is the foundation of any community. Events are still useful, but I think they work best when they take place in a shared space. For example, a garden could host a harvest day once a year, so the event strengthens relationships that the space has already started.
points: Chooses one side clearly and refers to Amara by name
Adds a new argument (spaces include shy, elderly or newcomer residents who avoid events)
Gives a concrete, step-by-step example of how trust develops
Shows balance by explaining how events could support the chosen option

stem: In environmental science this week, we are studying plastic pollution. Every year, millions of tons of plastic packaging end up in landfills and oceans, where they can remain for centuries. Communities have tried two broad approaches. Some ban certain single-use items, such as plastic bags and straws. Others keep these items legal but offer incentives, for example a small refund when people return bottles for recycling. Which approach do you think is more effective at reducing plastic waste, and why?

posts.name: Hamza
posts.text: Bans are more effective because they remove the problem completely. If shops are not allowed to give out plastic bags, people quickly get used to bringing their own. Incentives depend on people remembering to do the right thing, and many of them simply won't bother, especially when the refund is only a few cents.

posts.name: Olga
posts.text: I prefer incentives. Bans can create new problems, since some replacement products, like thick paper bags, also need a lot of energy to produce. A refund system keeps useful plastic items available but makes sure they are collected and recycled. In my home country, almost every bottle is returned because people see the money as their own.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on environmental science. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Olga that incentives are the better approach, although I would add a different reason. Bans only work for a small number of items that have easy substitutes, such as bags and straws. Most plastic waste, however, comes from packaging for food, cleaning products and electronics, which cannot simply be banned without causing serious problems for shops and customers. A refund system can be applied to a much wider range of products. Another advantage is that incentives create jobs and businesses. When large amounts of clean, sorted plastic are returned, recycling companies have a steady supply of material and can afford to invest in better technology. Hamza is right that a few cents may not motivate everyone, but the refund can be set high enough to make returning items worthwhile. In short, incentives can reach more types of plastic than bans ever could.
points: Takes a clear side and names Olga as the student it agrees with
Adds new reasons: bans cover only a few items, and incentives support the recycling industry
Responds to Hamza's concern by name instead of ignoring the other view
Finishes with a short summary sentence that restates the opinion

stem: In urban planning, one of the most debated questions is how to use limited street space. Many cities are now turning car lanes into protected bicycle lanes. Supporters say this makes streets safer and cleaner, while opponents point to heavier traffic and difficulties for businesses that rely on deliveries. Imagine your city is considering replacing one car lane on its main shopping street with a bike lane. Would you support this change? Explain why or why not.

posts.name: Yuki
posts.text: I would support it. Many people would like to cycle, but they are afraid of riding next to fast cars. A protected lane makes them feel safe, and once they start cycling, there are fewer cars on the road. In the end, traffic can actually improve because each cyclist is one less car looking for a parking space.

posts.name: Chen
posts.text: I would not support it on a shopping street. Shops need trucks to deliver goods every morning, and many customers drive in from other areas because they buy heavy items. If there is less space for cars, these customers may go to a large mall outside the city instead, and small local shops could lose a lot of business.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I understand Chen's worry about local shops, but I would support the bike lane. In fact, I think it could help businesses rather than hurt them. People on bicycles travel slowly enough to notice shop windows, and it is very easy for them to stop, lock their bike and go inside. Drivers, on the other hand, often pass by because they cannot find parking. As a result, cyclists and pedestrians may visit local shops more often, even if they spend a little less on each visit. The street would also become quieter and more pleasant, which encourages people to stay longer, sit in cafes and meet friends. To deal with deliveries, the city could allow trucks to load and unload in special zones early in the morning before the street gets busy. With careful planning, the main shopping street could become a place people enjoy visiting, not just driving through.
points: States support clearly and refers to Chen's opposing point by name
Adds a new argument: cyclists notice and stop at shops more easily than drivers
Offers a practical solution to the delivery problem
Uses cause-and-effect language ('As a result', 'which encourages') to develop ideas

stem: In our course on technology and society, we have been discussing how mobile phones affect young people's lives. Some schools now require students to lock their phones away from the start of the school day until it ends. Others allow phones during breaks or let teachers decide whether phones can be used for classwork. Do you think schools should ban students' phones for the whole school day, or should they allow phones at certain times? Explain your view.

posts.name: Aisha
posts.text: A full-day ban is the best option. Even during breaks, students who have phones tend to stare at their screens instead of talking or playing together. Without phones, break time becomes a chance to make friends and get some exercise, and students come back to class feeling more relaxed and ready to learn.

posts.name: Daniel
posts.text: I think phones should be allowed at some times. They can be useful learning tools, for example for looking up a word, taking a photo of the board or using a science app. Also, many parents want to be able to contact their children during the day, especially if plans change and someone else has to pick them up.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on technology and society. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Daniel makes a fair point about parents, but I support a full-day ban for most schools. The main reason, in my opinion, is that a clear rule is much easier to follow than a partial one. When phones are allowed at certain times, teachers must constantly check whether students are using them at the right moment, and arguments start over small things, such as sending one message just before the bell. A complete ban removes this daily conflict and lets teachers focus on teaching. Moreover, a ban reduces pressure on students who do not own expensive phones, because nobody can show off a new model at school. As for contacting children, parents can still call the school office in an emergency, just as families did before smartphones existed. If teachers need technology for a lesson, the school can provide tablets that are used only for learning.
points: Takes a clear position and refers to Daniel's argument by name
Adds new reasons: a simple rule is easier to enforce, and a ban reduces pressure about owning expensive phones
Answers the parent-contact concern with a realistic alternative
Keeps a polite, academic tone while disagreeing

stem: Our psychology unit this week is about motivation and goal setting. Some experts advise people to set ambitious long-term goals, such as running a marathon or becoming fluent in a language within a year, because a big target gives life direction. Others argue that it is better to focus on small daily habits, like jogging for ten minutes or learning five new words, without worrying about the final result. Which approach do you think leads to greater success, and why?

posts.name: Elena
posts.text: I believe big goals are more powerful. When I decided to pass a difficult exam, that clear target made me organize my whole week around studying. Small habits are nice, but without a larger purpose, it is easy to stop doing them when you are tired, because you don't see why they matter.

posts.name: Ravi
posts.text: For me, small habits work better. Big goals can feel so far away that people give up when they don't see quick progress. When I started doing just ten push-ups a day, it felt easy, so I never skipped it. Months later, I was much stronger than I had ever been with my old, ambitious plans.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on psychology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Ravi that small daily habits lead to greater success, but for a slightly different reason. In my view, the biggest advantage of habits is that they are easier to recover from when something goes wrong. Life is unpredictable: people get sick, travel or have a busy week at work. If someone's goal is to lose ten kilograms by summer and they miss two weeks, they may feel they have already failed and quit completely. With a habit, missing a day is a small problem, and they simply start again tomorrow. Habits also build a new identity. A person who walks every morning slowly begins to see themselves as an active person, and this belief makes healthy choices feel natural rather than forced. Elena is right that a goal provides direction, so perhaps the best plan is to choose a goal but measure success by whether the daily habit is completed.
points: States agreement with Ravi by name and promises a different reason
Develops a new idea: habits make it easier to recover from setbacks and shape identity
Uses a concrete example (missing two weeks of a weight-loss plan)
Acknowledges Elena's view and finishes with a balanced suggestion

stem: In public health, we often look for ways to help people become more physically active, since regular exercise lowers the risk of many diseases. Two common strategies are workplace programs, such as free gym memberships or walking challenges for employees, and changes to city design, such as safer sidewalks, parks and bike paths. If a city had money for only one of these strategies, which do you think would do more to increase physical activity among adults? Please explain your reasoning.

posts.name: Grace
posts.text: Workplace programs would have a bigger effect. Adults spend most of their week at work, so that is where we can reach them. When my mother's company started a step challenge with small prizes, almost everyone in her office joined, and many of them still walk at lunchtime even though the challenge ended long ago.

posts.name: Tariq
posts.text: I would choose city design. Workplace programs help only people with office jobs, but sidewalks and parks are available to everyone, including retired people and those who work at home. If walking to the shop is safe and pleasant, people exercise without even planning to, simply as part of their daily routine.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on public health. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Like Tariq, I would spend the money on city design, and I have an additional reason. Changes to the environment last for decades, while workplace programs depend on a company's budget each year. A new park or bike path can keep encouraging people to move for thirty or forty years, long after a gym membership offer has been cancelled. In addition, better city design benefits children. When parents feel that the streets are safe, they let their children walk or cycle to school, and children who grow up being active are more likely to stay active as adults. In this way, one investment improves the health of two generations. Grace's example shows that workplace challenges can work, but they reach a smaller group and may disappear when a company changes its priorities. For a city choosing only one strategy, the long-lasting option seems wiser.
points: Clearly chooses city design and connects to Tariq by name
Adds new reasons: environmental changes last for decades and also benefit children
Acknowledges Grace's example while explaining its limits
Concludes with a sentence that ties the reasons back to the question

stem: In media studies this week, we are examining how news organizations pay for their work. For years, most news websites were free and earned money from advertising. Today, many of them place their articles behind a paywall, which means readers must buy a subscription to read more than a few stories each month. Some people believe paywalls are necessary for good journalism, while others think news should be free for everyone. What is your opinion? Should news websites charge readers for access?

posts.name: Nadia
posts.text: Yes, they should charge. Investigating a serious story can take reporters months of work, and that is expensive. When news depends only on advertising, websites are tempted to publish shocking headlines just to get clicks. Subscriptions allow them to focus on careful, accurate reporting, because readers are paying for quality rather than for excitement.

posts.name: Omar
posts.text: I think news should remain free. Not everyone can afford several subscriptions, and students or people with low incomes would only have access to free sources, which are often less reliable. If important information is locked away, society becomes divided between people who are well informed and people who are not.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on media studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Nadia that news websites should be allowed to charge readers, although Omar's concern about fairness is important. One reason that has not been mentioned is independence. When a news organization depends on a few large advertisers, it may hesitate to publish stories that criticize those companies, because it fears losing their money. If thousands of ordinary readers pay a small amount each month, no single advertiser has that kind of power, and journalists can report more freely. At the same time, there are ways to keep paywalls fair. Many newspapers already offer cheap student subscriptions, and public libraries can provide free digital access to their members. Some websites also make urgent information, such as weather warnings or health advice, free for everyone. With these exceptions, paywalls can support high-quality journalism without leaving people with low incomes behind.
points: Takes a clear position and refers to both Nadia and Omar by name
Adds a new reason: reader payments make journalists less dependent on advertisers
Addresses the fairness concern with specific solutions (student rates, library access, free urgent news)
Organizes the response with a main argument followed by a qualification

stem: In our economics course, we have been studying the costs and benefits of tourism. Popular destinations earn a lot of money from visitors, but large crowds can also raise housing prices, damage historic sites and put pressure on public services. To manage this, some cities charge a small tourist tax for every night a visitor stays in a hotel. Do you think popular cities should charge a tourist tax? Explain why or why not.

posts.name: Isabel
posts.text: I think a tourist tax is a good idea. Tourists use roads, public toilets and rubbish collection just like residents, but residents pay for most of these services. A small fee, perhaps two or three dollars a night, would not stop anyone from visiting, and the money could be used to clean streets and repair old buildings.

posts.name: Jin
posts.text: I don't agree. Tourism already brings huge amounts of money to a city through hotels, restaurants and shops, and these businesses pay taxes. An extra fee makes the city look unwelcoming. For families on a tight budget, the tax adds up over a long holiday, and they might choose a cheaper destination instead.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: In my opinion, popular cities should charge a tourist tax, and I would add a point that neither Isabel nor Jin mentioned: the tax can be used to spread visitors more evenly. A city could charge a higher fee during the busiest summer months and a lower fee, or none at all, in the quieter season. This would encourage some travelers to come at a different time, which reduces crowds at famous sites and gives local businesses customers all year instead of only for a few weeks. I understand Jin's worry that families might choose another destination, but I doubt a small nightly fee is enough to change most people's plans, since flights and hotels cost far more. As long as the city explains clearly how the money is spent, for example on parks or museum repairs, visitors are likely to accept the tax as fair.
points: States a clear opinion and names both students
Adds a new idea: a seasonal tax can spread visitors across the year
Responds to Jin's objection by name with reasoning about relative costs
Suggests a condition (transparency about spending) that strengthens the argument

stem: This week in our education course, we are looking at different forms of assessment. Many instructors now give group projects, in which three or four students research a topic together and receive one shared grade. Other instructors prefer individual assignments, such as essays and exams, because they show exactly what each student has learned. Which type of assignment do you think better prepares students for life after university: group projects or individual assignments? Explain why.

posts.name: Fatima
posts.text: Group projects are better preparation. In almost every job, people have to work in teams, divide tasks and solve disagreements. University is a safe place to practice these skills. During my last group project, I learned how to lead meetings and how to give feedback politely, which I could never have learned by writing an essay alone.

posts.name: Marco
posts.text: I prefer individual assignments. In group projects, one or two students usually do most of the work while the others relax, and everyone still gets the same grade. That is unfair. Individual work makes each person responsible for their own learning, and employers want to know what you can do, not what your team did.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I side with Fatima that group projects are better preparation for life after university, but I would like to add another benefit. Group projects teach students to work with people who think differently. In an individual essay, I only have to convince myself that my ideas are good. In a group, I have to listen to classmates from other countries or other majors who may approach the problem in a completely different way. For example, in a marketing project, an engineering student in my group suggested testing our idea with a simple survey, which made our final presentation much stronger. This kind of cooperation is exactly what happens in international companies. Marco is right that some students avoid their share of the work, but instructors can solve this by asking each member to write a short report on what they did and grading part of the project individually.
points: Chooses group projects and names Fatima as the student it agrees with
Adds a new benefit: learning to work with people who think differently
Supports the idea with a short, specific example
Answers Marco's fairness concern by name with a practical grading solution

stem: In our business course, we are studying customer loyalty, which is the tendency of customers to keep buying from the same company. Loyal customers are valuable because they spend more over time and recommend the company to friends. Some managers believe loyalty depends mainly on product quality, while others think excellent customer service matters more. In your opinion, which is more important for keeping customers loyal: the quality of the product or the quality of the service? Please explain.

posts.name: Leila
posts.text: Product quality is more important. If a phone breaks after six months, it doesn't matter how friendly the staff were in the shop. Customers return to brands whose products are reliable and work well every day. Good service cannot make up for a poor product for very long.

posts.name: Samuel
posts.text: I think service matters more. These days, many products are very similar in quality and price, so service is what makes one company stand out. I keep using the same small bike shop because the owner remembers my name, gives honest advice and fixes small problems for free, even though bigger stores are cheaper.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on business. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Although Leila is right that a bad product will drive customers away, I agree with Samuel that service is more important for loyalty. My reason is that service matters most at the moment when something goes wrong. Every company makes mistakes eventually: a delivery arrives late, or a product has a defect. What customers remember is how the company responds. If an airline loses my suitcase but the staff apologize, keep me informed and deliver it to my hotel the same evening, I may actually trust that airline more than before. On the other hand, if I spend an hour on the phone and nobody helps me, I will probably never fly with them again, no matter how comfortable their seats are. In other words, quality may bring customers in the first time, but service is what turns a problem into a reason to stay.
points: States a clear position and refers to both Leila and Samuel by name
Adds a new argument: service matters most when something goes wrong
Uses a vivid example (a lost suitcase) with contrasting outcomes
Ends with a memorable summary sentence linking back to loyalty

stem: Our sociology class has been discussing how people learn the skills and values they need in life. In the past, young people learned mostly from older family members and neighbors. Today, many young people turn to friends of their own age, often through social media and online communities, for advice on everything from studying to careers. Do you think young people today learn more useful lessons from older generations or from their peers? Explain your opinion.

posts.name: Hana
posts.text: Older generations still offer the most useful lessons. My grandfather has lived through many changes and has solved problems that my friends have never faced, such as managing money during hard times or keeping a small business running. Experience like that cannot be replaced by advice from people who are just as young as I am.

posts.name: Victor
posts.text: I think peers are more useful today. The world is changing so quickly that much of the advice from older people is out of date. For example, when I chose my university course, my friends knew much more than my parents about new jobs in technology, online applications and which skills employers want now.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Victor has a point about technology, but I agree with Hana that older generations offer the more useful lessons. In my view, the most valuable things older people teach are not technical skills but ways of dealing with people. My aunt, for instance, taught me how to calm down before answering an angry message and how to apologize properly when I am wrong. These lessons do not become out of date, because human relationships have not changed very much, even if the tools we use to communicate have. Peers, by contrast, often have the same blind spots as we do, since they are at the same stage of life and are dealing with similar worries. Their advice can feel comforting, but it rarely challenges us. Older people have seen how similar situations ended, so they can warn us about consequences that young people cannot yet imagine.
points: Takes Hana's side clearly while acknowledging Victor by name
Adds a new reason: older people teach lasting lessons about relationships
Explains a weakness of peer advice (shared blind spots)
Uses a personal example to make the argument concrete

stem: In environmental science, we have been studying how to protect endangered animal species. One approach is to breed animals in zoos and wildlife centers and later return some of them to the wild. Another approach is to protect the natural habitats where these animals live, for example by creating national parks and limiting logging or farming nearby. If a conservation organization could fund only one of these approaches, which do you think it should choose, and why?

posts.name: Ingrid
posts.text: The organization should protect habitats. Even if a zoo breeds hundreds of animals, they have nowhere to go if their forest or wetland has been destroyed. Protecting a habitat also saves many other species at the same time, including plants and insects that zoos never pay attention to.

posts.name: Kenji
posts.text: I would fund breeding programs. When a species has only a few dozen animals left, protecting land is too slow to save it. Zoos can keep a population safe from disease and hunting while scientists study it. Some animals that were almost extinct in the wild survived only because they were bred in captivity.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on environmental science. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Ingrid that protecting habitats is the better choice, and I would add an economic reason. Breeding programs are very expensive for each animal, because the animals need special food, veterinary care and large enclosures for many years. The same amount of money could protect a large area of land, and protected areas can even earn money of their own. For example, many national parks attract visitors who pay entrance fees and hire local guides, which gives nearby communities a reason to keep the forest healthy instead of cutting it down. This makes habitat protection more sustainable over the long term. Kenji is correct that captive breeding can rescue a species in an emergency, but it should be a last resort. If we protect habitats early, fewer species will ever reach the point where they can survive only in a zoo.
points: Supports habitat protection and names Ingrid
Adds a new economic argument: lower cost per animal and income from visitors
Acknowledges Kenji's point by name and explains its limits
Closes with a forward-looking idea (preventing emergencies)

stem: Growing cities need more housing, and urban planners must decide where and how to build it. One option is to build upward, with tall apartment buildings in or near the city center. Another option is to build outward, creating new neighborhoods of houses with gardens on the edge of the city. Each choice affects transportation, the environment and people's quality of life. In your view, which option should a growing city choose, and why?

posts.name: Lina
posts.text: Cities should build upward. Tall buildings use much less land, so forests and farmland around the city can be protected. When many people live close together near the center, it also becomes practical to run frequent buses and trains, and people can walk to work, shops and schools instead of driving everywhere.

posts.name: Diego
posts.text: I think building outward is better for families. Many parents want a house with a garden where children can play safely. Apartments in the city center are often small and expensive, while new neighborhoods on the edge can offer more space for the same price, which improves people's quality of life.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Lina that a growing city should build upward, and I would like to add a reason related to public costs. Every new neighborhood on the edge of a city needs new roads, water pipes, electricity lines, schools and fire stations. These are extremely expensive to build and maintain, and the cost is shared by all taxpayers, including people who live in the center. Tall buildings, in contrast, can use infrastructure that already exists. A city that builds upward therefore spends less money on construction and has more to spend on parks, libraries and public transport. Diego's point about families is understandable, but tall buildings do not have to mean small, dark apartments. Planners can require larger family apartments, shared courtyards and playgrounds on the ground floor, so that children still have safe places to play close to home.
points: Chooses one option clearly and refers to Lina by name
Adds a new reason: building outward requires costly new infrastructure
Responds to Diego's concern by name with concrete design solutions
Uses contrast words ('in contrast', 'therefore') to structure the argument

stem: In technology and society, we have been exploring how artificial intelligence is changing education. Several apps now act as personal tutors: they explain problems step by step, answer questions at any hour and adjust exercises to each learner's level. Some people predict that these tools will greatly reduce the need for human tutors. Others believe that human tutors offer something technology cannot. For a high school student who needs extra help in math, would an AI tutor or a human tutor be more helpful? Why?

posts.name: Zara
posts.text: An AI tutor would be more helpful. It is available whenever the student is stuck, even late at night before a test, and it never gets impatient when the same question is asked five times. It is also much cheaper than a human tutor, so more families could afford regular help.

posts.name: Felix
posts.text: A human tutor is better. Many students who struggle with math are not just confused about the steps; they are nervous and have lost confidence. A good human tutor notices when a student is frustrated, encourages them and changes the lesson. An app cannot really understand how a teenager feels.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on technology and society. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Felix that a human tutor would be more helpful, but my reason is a little different. I think the biggest advantage of a human tutor is accountability. When a student knows that a real person is expecting them on Tuesday at five o'clock and will ask whether they finished their practice problems, they are much more likely to do the work. An app, on the other hand, is easy to ignore; the student can simply close it when the questions get difficult, and nobody will notice. Many teenagers know they should study, but they need someone to keep them on track. Zara is right that AI tutors are cheaper and always available, so I think they work best as an extra tool between sessions. For a student who is really struggling, however, regular meetings with a human tutor provide the structure and commitment that make improvement possible.
points: Takes a clear position and names Felix
Introduces a new reason: a human tutor creates accountability
Explains why an app is easy to ignore, giving a realistic picture
Acknowledges Zara's view by name and suggests a combined approach

stem: In our psychology course, we are studying decision making. Some research suggests that groups make better decisions because members share knowledge and catch each other's mistakes. Other research shows that groups sometimes make worse choices, for example when people agree with the majority simply to avoid conflict. Think about important decisions, such as choosing a strategy for a project or planning a major purchase. Do you think people generally make better decisions alone or in a group? Explain your view.

posts.name: Beatriz
posts.text: Groups make better decisions. Each person sees a problem from a different angle, so a group can think of more options and notice risks that one person might miss. When my family planned a long trip, my brother realized our passports needed renewing, something I had completely forgotten while I was busy comparing hotels.

posts.name: Arjun
posts.text: I think people decide better alone. In groups, the loudest person often controls the discussion, and quieter people keep their good ideas to themselves. Group decisions also take much longer. When I work alone, I can collect information, think carefully and make a choice without wasting hours in meetings.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on psychology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I believe groups generally make better decisions, as Beatriz suggests, but only if they are organized well. Arjun is right that loud members can dominate a meeting, yet this problem has a simple solution: each person can write down their own ideas before the discussion starts. This way, quiet members contribute, and nobody is influenced by the majority too early. Another benefit of groups that has not been mentioned is commitment. When people help make a decision, they understand the reasons behind it and feel responsible for its success. For instance, if a team chooses its own project schedule, members are more likely to meet the deadlines than if a manager simply announces the plan. A person deciding alone may choose quickly, but if others have to carry out the decision, they may not support it fully. For important decisions that affect several people, a well-run group is the wiser choice.
points: States a position with a clear condition ('only if they are organized well')
Responds to Arjun by name with a specific technique (writing ideas first)
Adds a new reason: people commit more to decisions they helped make
Includes an example and a concluding sentence linked to the question

stem: This week in public health, we are discussing young people's diets. Many teenagers drink several sugary drinks a day, which is linked to tooth decay and weight gain. Schools have tried different responses. Some have removed sugary drinks from their cafeterias and vending machines entirely. Others still sell them but display clear information about sugar content and offer cheaper healthy alternatives, such as water and milk. Which approach do you think is better for students' health, and why?

posts.name: Chloe
posts.text: Removing sugary drinks is the better approach. Teenagers often choose what tastes good, not what is healthy, even when they know the facts. If the drinks are simply not available at school, students drink water instead, and over time they may lose the habit of having soda with every meal.

posts.name: Mohammed
posts.text: I prefer giving information and cheaper alternatives. If schools remove these drinks, students will just buy them at the shop across the street. Teaching them to read labels and make good choices is more useful, because after they leave school, nobody will be there to remove unhealthy products for them.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on public health. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Chloe that schools should remove sugary drinks completely, and I want to add a point about the message schools send. A school is supposed to teach healthy habits in its science and sports classes. If the same school then sells soda in the cafeteria, students receive mixed messages, and the lessons seem less serious. Removing the drinks shows that the school really believes what it teaches. Mohammed makes a fair argument about the shop across the street, but I do not think most students would leave campus every day just to buy a drink, especially younger ones who are not allowed to go out at lunchtime. Even if some do, the total amount of sugar they consume would still fall. Of course, schools should also teach students to read food labels, but this education works best when the school environment supports it instead of contradicting it.
points: Takes Chloe's side and names her clearly
Adds a new idea: selling sugary drinks sends a mixed message about health
Answers Mohammed's argument by name with realistic reasoning
Shows balance by including label education as a support, not a replacement

stem: In media studies, we have been looking at how online reviews influence what people buy. Before choosing a restaurant, hotel or product, many consumers now read ratings and comments written by strangers. Supporters say that reviews give ordinary people power and push companies to improve. Critics point out that some reviews are fake, paid for, or written by people who are simply in a bad mood. Overall, do you think online reviews help consumers make better choices, or do they mislead them more often than they help?

posts.name: Sven
posts.text: Online reviews mostly help. When I booked a hotel last summer, several reviews mentioned that the rooms facing the street were very noisy, so I asked for a quiet room. That kind of detail never appears in an advertisement. With hundreds of reviews, a few fake ones don't change the overall picture.

posts.name: Maya
posts.text: I think reviews are often misleading. People usually write reviews only when they are extremely happy or extremely angry, so the ratings don't show the normal experience. I once avoided a cafe because of a few terrible reviews, but when a friend took me there, the food and service were excellent.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on media studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Maya is right that extreme opinions appear more often, but I still believe online reviews help consumers more than they mislead them. One benefit that hasn't been mentioned is the way companies respond in public. Many businesses now reply to complaints online, and these replies tell me a lot. If a restaurant answers a negative review politely and explains how it fixed the problem, I feel more confident eating there. If it attacks the customer, I know to stay away. This conversation between customers and businesses did not exist before review websites. In addition, careful readers can avoid most of the problems Maya describes. Instead of looking only at the star rating, I read several reviews from the middle of the scale, which usually describe the normal experience in a calm way. When reviews are read thoughtfully, they are one of the most useful tools a modern consumer has.
points: Clearly states that reviews help more than they mislead
Adds a new argument: public replies from businesses reveal how they treat customers
Responds to Maya by name and explains a reading strategy that answers her concern
Uses a balanced, reasoned tone with concrete examples

stem: In our economics course, we are studying how companies try to influence consumer behavior. Many supermarkets, airlines and coffee shops run loyalty programs, which give customers points, discounts or free items in exchange for repeat purchases. These programs are extremely common, but economists disagree about who really gains from them. Do you think loyalty programs mainly benefit consumers, or do they mainly benefit the companies that run them? Explain your opinion.

posts.name: Rosa
posts.text: Loyalty programs mainly benefit consumers. My family shops at the same supermarket every week anyway, so the points we collect are basically free money. Last year we saved enough to get a large discount on a new kettle. If you are going to buy something regularly, it makes sense to be rewarded for it.

posts.name: Ethan
posts.text: Companies are the real winners. The rewards are usually small, but they persuade people to keep shopping at one store even when another store has lower prices. Customers end up paying more overall, and they often buy extra products just to reach the next reward level.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Ethan that loyalty programs mainly benefit companies, and I would add one more reason: data. Every time customers scan a loyalty card, the company records what they bought, when and how often. This information is extremely valuable. It allows the company to decide which products to stock, how to set prices and which personal offers will tempt each customer to spend more. In a sense, customers are paying for their small discounts with detailed information about their own habits, and most of them never think about it. Rosa is right that families who shop regularly can save some money, and I do not think people should stop using these programs. However, the fact that nearly every large company offers one suggests that the programs earn them far more than they give away. Otherwise, businesses would not continue investing so much in them.
points: Takes Ethan's position and refers to him by name
Adds a new reason: companies gain valuable data about customer habits
Acknowledges Rosa's experience by name and keeps a fair tone
Uses logical reasoning ('Otherwise, businesses would not...') to support the conclusion

stem: In our education course, we are discussing the transition from high school to university. In some countries, it is common for students to take a gap year, a year away from formal study to work, travel or volunteer before starting university. Supporters say it helps students mature and choose the right field. Critics say it delays students' careers and that many never return to study. Would you recommend that students take a gap year before university? Why or why not?

posts.name: Noor
posts.text: I would recommend it. Many eighteen-year-olds choose a university major without really knowing what they want, and some change subjects after wasting a year or two. Working or volunteering for a year gives them real experience, so they can make a better decision and start university with clearer goals.

posts.name: Patrick
posts.text: I wouldn't recommend it. After a year away, it is hard to get back into the habit of studying, and students may forget a lot of what they learned in school, especially in subjects like math. They also start earning a full salary a year later than their classmates.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on education. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I would recommend a gap year, as Noor does, but for an additional reason: it teaches independence. Many students go straight from living with their parents to living in a university dormitory, where meals, schedules and support services are all organized for them. A student who has spent a year working in a cafe or volunteering in another city learns to manage money, solve problems alone and deal with adults in a professional way. These skills make the first year of university much less stressful, and students who feel confident are more likely to stay in their program. Patrick's concern about forgetting math is reasonable, but students can avoid it by taking a short online course or reviewing for a few weeks before classes begin. One year is a small part of a long career, and the maturity gained during that year can make the rest of a student's education more successful.
points: Gives a clear recommendation and names Noor as the student it agrees with
Adds a new reason: a gap year builds independence and practical life skills
Responds to Patrick's concern by name with a simple solution
Ends by putting the cost (one year) into perspective

stem: This week in business, we are studying entrepreneurship. People who start a new company face many early decisions, and one of the most important is whether to start alone or with one or more co-founders. Working alone means full control, while a partner brings extra skills, money and support but also the possibility of disagreement. If you were starting a small business, such as an online clothing shop or a cafe, would you rather start it alone or with a partner? Explain your choice.

posts.name: Camila
posts.text: I would choose a partner. Running a business involves many different jobs, like marketing, accounting and dealing with suppliers, and nobody is good at everything. If my partner is skilled in the areas where I am weak, the business has a much better chance. We could also share the stress during difficult months.

posts.name: Ahmed
posts.text: I would rather start alone. Partners often disagree about important things, like how fast to grow or how to spend profits, and these arguments can destroy both the business and the friendship. When I am the only owner, I can make quick decisions and keep all the profits for myself.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on business. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Ahmed's worry about disagreements is understandable, but I would still start a business with a partner, as Camila suggests. One reason that has not been mentioned is that a partner helps you see your own mistakes. When you work alone, nobody questions your ideas, so it is easy to become too excited about a plan that will not work. For example, if I wanted to open a cafe in a quiet street because the rent is cheap, a partner might point out that very few customers would ever walk past it. A second opinion like this can prevent expensive errors in the early months, when a small business has very little money to lose. To reduce the risk of conflict, partners should agree in writing from the beginning how decisions will be made and what will happen if one of them wants to leave. With clear rules, a partnership offers far more benefits than problems.
points: States a clear choice and refers to both students by name
Adds a new reason: a partner can question your ideas and prevent costly mistakes
Gives a concrete example (a cafe on a quiet street)
Responds to the risk of conflict with a practical suggestion

stem: Our sociology class is studying volunteering and civic participation. Some high schools require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours, for example forty hours at a hospital, library or community center, before they can graduate. Supporters say this teaches responsibility and connects young people with their communities. Others argue that volunteering loses its meaning when it is forced. Do you think high schools should require volunteer work for graduation? Explain your view.

posts.name: Lucia
posts.text: Yes, it should be required. Many teenagers would never think of volunteering on their own, but once they try it, they often enjoy it. My cousin had to volunteer at an animal shelter for school, and now, three years later, she still goes there every weekend because she discovered how much she loves helping.

posts.name: Kai
posts.text: I don't think it should be required. Volunteering should come from a real wish to help. If students are forced, many will just do the minimum and watch the clock, which doesn't help the organization much. Also, some students already work part-time to support their families and simply don't have the extra time.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on sociology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Lucia that high schools should require volunteer work, and I would add that it helps students explore possible careers. A teenager who volunteers at a hospital may discover a strong interest in nursing, while another who helps at a library might realize they enjoy teaching children to read. These experiences are difficult to get any other way at that age, because most employers will not hire students without experience. Volunteering also gives students something real to write about in university applications and to discuss in job interviews. Kai raises an important point about students who already work, so I think schools should be flexible. For instance, they could reduce the required hours for students with family responsibilities or allow them to volunteer during school holidays. With this flexibility, the requirement would open doors for young people without being unfair to anyone.
points: Takes a clear position and names Lucia
Adds a new reason: volunteering helps students explore careers and strengthens applications
Responds to Kai's concern by name with specific flexible options
Uses examples from different volunteer settings to support the argument

stem: In environmental science, we are studying the urban heat island effect. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside because roads and buildings absorb heat during the day and release it at night. Two common solutions are planting many more trees along streets and covering roofs with light-colored materials that reflect sunlight. If a city wanted to reduce summer heat and had money for only one of these solutions, which should it choose? Explain why.

posts.name: Emma
posts.text: The city should plant trees. Trees provide shade for people walking on the street, which makes a huge difference on a hot afternoon. They also clean the air and make neighborhoods more beautiful. A reflective roof might cool a building, but it does nothing for someone waiting at a bus stop in the sun.

posts.name: Wei
posts.text: Reflective roofs are the better choice. Trees take many years to grow large enough to give real shade, and they need water and care. Reflective roofs work from the first day. They also lower the temperature inside buildings, so people use less air conditioning, which saves money and electricity.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on environmental science. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Wei makes a good point about how quickly reflective roofs work, but I would choose trees, like Emma. One benefit she did not mention is that trees help with heavy rain as well as heat. Their roots and the soil around them absorb water, so streets flood less during summer storms. In many cities, hot summers and sudden storms happen together, so one investment can solve two problems. Trees also last for decades, while roof coatings slowly get dirty and lose their ability to reflect sunlight unless they are cleaned or replaced. It is true that young trees need time to grow, but the city could start with fast-growing species in the hottest neighborhoods and plant more each year. In the long run, trees provide shade, cleaner air and better protection from flooding, which makes them more valuable than reflective roofs.
points: Chooses trees clearly and refers to both Emma and Wei
Adds a new reason: trees also reduce flooding from heavy rain
Answers the 'trees grow slowly' concern with a practical plan
Concludes by summarizing the combined benefits

stem: In urban planning, we have been examining how cities use their historic centers. Several cities have started closing the central streets to cars on weekends, turning them into spaces for walking, cycling, markets and street performances. Some residents love the change, while others complain that it makes it harder to reach the center, especially for older people. Would you support closing your city center to cars every weekend? Explain why or why not.

posts.name: Tomas
posts.text: I would support it. Without traffic, the center becomes quieter and safer, and families can relax there without worrying about their children running into the road. Local shops and cafes can put tables outside, and markets and musicians give people a reason to visit the center instead of staying at home.

posts.name: Ayesha
posts.text: I would not support it every weekend. Weekends are when many people do their shopping and visit relatives in the center. Older people, people with disabilities and parents with small children often depend on cars. If they cannot drive into the center, they may stop going there at all.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I would support closing the city center to cars on weekends, as Tomas does, and I would add a benefit related to history and culture. Many city centers contain old buildings, fountains and small squares that people hardly notice when they are busy watching for traffic. On a car-free weekend, residents and tourists can slow down, look around and learn about their city's past. Museums and guides could even offer free walking tours on those days. In addition, less traffic means less pollution, which helps protect old stone buildings from damage over time. Ayesha's concern about older people and those with disabilities is very important, but it can be solved. The city could run free electric shuttles from parking areas at the edge of the center and allow special permits for people who need a car. With these services, everyone could enjoy a calmer, more attractive city center.
points: Supports the idea clearly and refers to Tomas and Ayesha by name
Adds a new reason: car-free streets help people appreciate and protect historic buildings
Responds to the accessibility concern with practical solutions (shuttles, permits)
Keeps the response organized: position, new reason, response to the other view

stem: In technology and society, we are looking at how digital tools are changing the way students read. Many universities now offer digital textbooks, which are often cheaper and can be read on a laptop, tablet or phone. However, some students still prefer printed books and say they understand and remember more when they read on paper. For university courses, do you think digital textbooks or printed textbooks are the better choice for students? Explain your answer.

posts.name: Julia
posts.text: Digital textbooks are better. They are usually much cheaper, and students can carry all their books on one device instead of a heavy backpack. They also have useful tools, like searching for a key word in seconds or making the text larger, which is very helpful when you are reviewing for an exam.

posts.name: Bilal
posts.text: I prefer printed textbooks. When I read on a screen, I constantly get notifications and end up checking messages instead of studying. With a paper book, I can focus for a longer time, and writing notes in the margins helps me remember where important information is on the page.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on technology and society. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Julia lists some real advantages, but I agree with Bilal that printed textbooks are the better choice for university courses. Besides the problem of distractions, there is the issue of eye strain. University students already spend many hours a day looking at screens for online assignments, emails and lectures. Adding long reading sessions on a laptop can cause headaches and tired eyes, which makes it harder to concentrate in the evening. Reading on paper gives the eyes a break. Printed books can also be shared or sold to next year's students, while many digital textbooks expire after one semester and cannot be passed on to anyone. This means the price difference is often smaller than it first appears. For short articles or quick searches, digital texts are convenient, but for the main textbook that students must study carefully all semester, paper is still the more effective option.
points: Takes Bilal's side clearly while acknowledging Julia by name
Adds new reasons: eye strain from screen time and the resale value of printed books
Challenges the cost argument with a specific point (digital access expiring)
Finishes with a qualified conclusion that shows careful thinking

stem: Our psychology unit this week is about attention and learning. Many students listen to music while they study, and they say it helps them relax and stay focused. However, some researchers believe that music, especially songs with lyrics, competes with the brain's ability to process new information. Based on your own experience and knowledge, do you think listening to music while studying helps students or makes their studying less effective? Explain why.

posts.name: Adriana
posts.text: Music helps me study. The library is often silent in a way that makes me feel sleepy, and at home I can hear my neighbors talking. Soft music covers those noises and puts me in a calm mood, so I can work for two hours without feeling bored or stressed.

posts.name: Musa
posts.text: I think music makes studying less effective. When I play songs I like, I start singing along in my head and lose track of what I am reading. I may feel productive, but when I try to remember the material the next day, I realize I didn't really absorb it.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on psychology. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: In my opinion, whether music helps depends on the type of studying, but for most serious learning I agree with Musa that it makes studying less effective. One point that has not been mentioned is the difference between studying and taking the exam. If students always review with music playing, the room will feel very different during the test, which happens in complete silence. Some people find it harder to remember information in a setting that does not match the one where they learned it. Practicing in quiet conditions prepares them better for the real exam. That said, Adriana's experience is valid for certain tasks. Music without lyrics can make repetitive work, such as organizing notes or copying formulas, more pleasant. So my advice would be to turn the music off when reading or memorizing new material and to save it for the simpler parts of studying.
points: Gives a clear, qualified position and refers to Musa by name
Adds a new reason: studying in silence matches the conditions of the real exam
Acknowledges Adriana by name and identifies tasks where music may help
Ends with practical advice that follows logically from the argument

stem: In public health, we have been studying sleep, which affects memory, mood and physical health. Surveys show that many teenagers sleep far less than the eight to ten hours experts recommend. Some schools have responded by starting classes later in the morning. Others focus on educating families, for example by encouraging parents to keep phones and tablets out of bedrooms at night. Which approach do you think would do more to help teenagers get enough sleep, and why?

posts.name: Sara
posts.text: Starting school later would help more. Teenagers' body clocks naturally make them feel awake late at night, so even if they go to bed early, they often can't fall asleep. If classes started an hour later, they could get the extra sleep they need without fighting against their own biology.

posts.name: Liam
posts.text: I think removing screens from bedrooms would help more. Many teenagers stay up watching videos or chatting with friends until after midnight. If school started later, they would probably just stay up even later. The real problem is the phone next to the bed, not the time school begins.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on public health. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Sara that starting school later would do more to help teenagers sleep, and I would add a practical reason. A later start time is one decision made by the school, and it affects every student at once. Educating families, on the other hand, depends on thousands of separate homes. Some parents will follow the advice, but others work night shifts, are too busy to check, or simply do not agree, so the results would be very uneven. A schedule change also helps with travel. In many areas, students catch a bus before seven o'clock, which means waking up extremely early even if they went to bed on time. Liam is right that phones keep teenagers awake, and schools could still teach good sleep habits in health classes. But a policy that reaches everyone automatically is more likely to make a real difference than advice that families may ignore.
points: Chooses one approach and names Sara
Adds a new argument: a school-wide policy reaches every student, while family advice is uneven
Includes a concrete detail (early bus times) to support the opinion
Acknowledges Liam's point by name and shows how both ideas can work together

stem: In media studies, we are examining how young people follow current events. A growing number of people under twenty-five now get most of their news from short videos lasting one or two minutes. Others still prefer longer articles from newspapers or news websites. Each format has strengths and weaknesses. Which do you think is a better way for young people to stay informed about the world: short news videos or longer written articles? Explain your choice.

posts.name: Jae
posts.text: Short videos are better for young people. Most of us are busy with classes and jobs, and we don't have time to read long articles every day. A two-minute video gives the main facts quickly, and seeing real images makes the story easier to understand and remember than reading a page of text.

posts.name: Clara
posts.text: Longer articles are better. Important events are usually complicated, and a two-minute video can only show one small part of the story. Articles explain the background, give different points of view and include facts and numbers. Without that information, viewers may form strong opinions about something they don't really understand.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on media studies. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: Jae is right that videos are quick and easy to understand, but I agree with Clara that longer articles are a better way to stay informed. Another reason is that articles make it easier to check where information comes from. A good article names its sources, quotes experts and often links to original reports, so readers can confirm the facts for themselves. Short videos, in contrast, are frequently copied and shared by accounts that nobody knows, and it can be very difficult to tell whether the clip is recent, complete or even real. For example, an old video of a flood might be shared as if it happened yesterday. Reading articles also improves young people's vocabulary and concentration, which helps them in their studies. Short videos can be a useful way to discover a story, but young people should then read a full article to understand it properly.
points: States a clear preference and refers to both Jae and Clara by name
Adds a new reason: articles make it easier to check sources and accuracy
Gives a specific example of how short videos can mislead
Ends with a balanced recommendation combining both formats

stem: In our economics course, we have been looking at the competition between small local shops and large chain stores. In many towns, family-owned bookshops, bakeries and hardware stores have closed because they cannot match the low prices of national chains and online retailers. Some towns now offer small businesses lower rent or tax reductions to help them survive. Do you think towns should use public money to support small local shops? Why or why not?

posts.name: Hassan
posts.text: Yes, towns should support them. Local shops give a town its character. When every main street has the same chain stores, towns all start to look the same. Family businesses also know their customers personally and often sponsor local sports teams and school events, which strengthens the community.

posts.name: Mia
posts.text: I don't think public money should be used this way. If customers prefer the lower prices of chain stores, that is their choice. Supporting shops that cannot compete means taxpayers pay to keep them open, and that money could be spent on things everyone needs, like schools or road repairs.

task: Your professor is teaching a class on economics. Write a post responding to the professor's question. In your response, you should do the following: express and support your opinion, and make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words.
explanation: I agree with Hassan that towns should support small local shops, and I want to add an economic argument. When people spend money at a family-owned business, much more of that money stays in the town. The owner lives locally, hires local workers and often buys supplies from other nearby businesses, such as a bakery that buys flour from a regional mill. A large chain, by contrast, sends much of its profit to headquarters in another city. Supporting local shops therefore helps other businesses and jobs in the same town. Mia makes a reasonable point that taxpayers' money is limited, so I think the support should be modest and temporary. For example, a town could reduce rent on empty shop spaces for a new business's first two years. This gives small shops a fair chance to establish themselves without creating permanent costs for taxpayers.
points: Takes a clear position and names Hassan
Adds a new economic reason: money spent locally circulates within the town
Acknowledges Mia's concern by name and limits the proposal (modest, temporary support)
Uses a concrete example to make the proposal realistic
